content.intro: This lesson covers Input Validation and Defensive Programming. It sits in Module 24, Security, Reliability, and Production Engineering, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Input Validation and Defensive Programming matters when you work with robust interaction with external resources. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Production reliability requires validating untrusted inputs, managing failures explicitly, controlling dependencies and secrets, recording useful diagnostics, and rehearsing recovery and shutdown behavior.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Input Validation and Defensive Programming, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Secure production software limits trust, validates inputs at boundaries, protects configuration, monitors failure, and has a repeatable release/rollback process.

fn safe_label(text: &str) -> bool { !text.is_empty() && text.len() <= 32 && text.chars().all(|c| c.is_ascii_alphanumeric() || c == '-') }

content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the Rust sample as src/main.rs in a Cargo project and run cargo run. Review the expected output, then change one input to explore an edge case.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Return the sample to its original form, run the documented command again, and compare the result. If a dependency, target, runtime, database, or hardware device is required, configure that separately before treating the result as verified.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not assume Input Validation and Defensive Programming guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.

content_blocks.title: Toolchain and execution boundary
content_blocks.text: Course examples are static reference snippets, not executed inside CodeLeaf. Most standard-library examples can be tried in a Rust 2024 Cargo project; specialized networking, database, async, procedural-macro, embedded, and WebAssembly scenarios require the toolchain and dependencies described in their lessons.
